==Legal issues==
===2005–2006===
During the 2005 draft, Jones was on [[probation]] for a fight in [[West Virginia]]. He encountered more legal trouble before playing a down for the Titans. On July 14, 2005, Jones was arrested on charges of [[assault]] and [[felony]] [[vandalism]] stemming from a [[nightclub]] altercation in [[Nashville, Tennessee|Nashville]]. On September 5, 2005, police were involved when Jones was belligerent after being told to wait in line for his vehicle at the annual Nashville Sports Council Kickoff luncheon where he was a guest. He refused to pay for [[valet]] services used that evening, claiming he had no cash in possession.

The state of West Virginia filed a petition, alleging that Jones had not made regular and sufficient contact with his [[probation]] officer or reported his July arrest in a timely fashion. The court ordered Jones' probation extended for 90 days.

In February 2006, Jones was arrested in [[Fayetteville, Georgia]], after an incident outside a home. Charges of marijuana possession were quickly dismissed, but the state pressed charges for felony and misdemeanor counts of obstruction of justice.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=2784050 |title=Pacman faces obstruction charge in Georgia|publisher=ESPN|agency=Associated Press |access-date=October 14, 2008}}</ref>

A Cadillac with Jones' nickname "Pacman" stitched in the headrests was seized during an April 2006 cocaine bust. The car was not registered to Jones at that time, but Jones told a local TV reporter it was his car and that he had loaned it to Darryl Moore for a music video. Police sources confirmed that Moore was the main target of their investigation. Jones later bought the car at a police auction.<ref name="red-cadillac">[[Associated Press]], [https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=2682645 Report: Titans' CB wins seized 'Pacman' car in auction], December 1, 2006.</ref>

On August 25, 2006, during training camp, Jones was arrested in [[Murfreesboro, Tennessee|Murfreesboro]], [[Tennessee]], for disorderly conduct and public intoxication at a nightclub after he spat on a woman he accused of stealing his wallet. Police said that the staff at the nightclub ordered Jones to leave several times, but he refused, continuing to shout profanities at the woman. A judge gave Jones six months probation on the condition he stay out of trouble and away from the nightclub.<ref name="nightclub">[https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=2727784 Charges will be dropped if Pacman stays out of trouble], ESPN.com, January 11, 2007.</ref> On October 26, 2006, Jones was cited for misdemeanor assault for allegedly spitting in the face of a female [[Tennessee State University]] student during a private party at Club Mystic, a Nashville nightclub. He was suspended by the Titans for one game.

===Las Vegas shooting case and suspension===
On the morning of February 19, 2007, during the [[2007 NBA All-Star Game]] weekend in Las Vegas, Jones was allegedly involved in an altercation with an [[exotic dancer]] at Minxx, a local [[strip club]]. Jones and American [[Rapping|rap artist]] [[Nelly]], along with another patron known as Richard Rich, showered the stage with hundreds of $1 bills. Club promoter Chris Mitchell then directed his dancers to pick up the money. According to the club's co-owner, Jones became enraged when a dancer began taking the money without his permission. He allegedly grabbed her by her hair and slammed her head on the stage. A security guard intervened and scuffled with members of Jones' entourage. Jones then allegedly threatened the guard's life.<ref name="strippers">{{cite news|url=http://www.reviewjournal.com/lvrj_home/2007/Feb-22-Thu-2007/news/12741485.html|title=Warrant includes details of club melee, shootings|publisher=Las Vegas Review-Journal|date=February 22, 2007|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070224123406/http://www.reviewjournal.com/lvrj_home/2007/Feb-22-Thu-2007/news/12741485.html|archive-date=February 24, 2007}}</ref> During this time, Mitchell and a male associate left the club with a garbage bag filled with $81,020 in cash and two [[Breitling SA|Breitling]] watches, which police later recovered.<ref name="amount">[https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=2775250 Police: Pacman's cash display sparked Vegas melee], ESPN, February 23, 2007.</ref> After club patrons left following the original confrontation, the club owner claimed that a person in Jones' entourage returned with a gun and fired into a crowd, damaging equipment and striking three people, including a security guard. The guard was shot twice, and one of the people hit—former professional wrestler Tommy Urbanski—was paralyzed from the waist down. Jones maintained that he did not know the shooter, although the club's owner insisted that Jones did. On March 26, 2007, the [[Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department]] recommended to the city's district attorney that Jones would be charged with one count of felony coercion, one misdemeanor count of battery and one misdemeanor count of threat to life.<ref name="charges">{{cite web|url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=2813615 |title=Pacman Jones could face misdemeanors, felony |work=ESPN.com |date=March 27, 2007 |access-date=November 16, 2021}}</ref>

More trouble followed Jones after the altercation, when drug dealer Darryl Moore was arrested. Wiretapped phone conversations between Moore and his friends revealed Moore talking about how Jones bet on college games to earn quick money. "You know, I was talking to him the other day about smoking, and he was like 'man, if I didn't smoke I couldn't take all the stress that I'm dealing with right now,'" Moore said.<ref name="newschannel">[http://www.newschannel5.com/Global/story.asp?S=6146420 Drug Dealer's Recorded Calls Mention Pacman's Troubles] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070927201717/http://www.newschannel5.com/Global/story.asp?S=6146420 |date=September 27, 2007 }}, NewsChannel5.com ([[Nashville, Tennessee|Nashville]]), February 27, 2007.</ref>

On June 20, 2007, the Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department and [[Clark County, Nevada|Clark County]] District Attorney's office announced that Jones would face two felony charges stemming from the February strip club melee.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=2910497|title= Pacman faces felony charges in shooting that paralyzed man|access-date=November 16, 2021|publisher=ESPN|agency=Associated Press}}</ref> On November 13, 2007, Jones accepted a plea deal,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.espn.com/espn/wire?section=nfl&id=3107824|title='Pacman' Jones to take plea deal in Vegas club triple shooting|last=Walker|first=Teresa M.|date=November 13, 2007|publisher=ESPN|access-date=November 16, 2021}}</ref> and on December 6 Jones pleaded no contest to one charge of conspiracy to commit disorderly conduct, a misdemeanor. He was given a suspended prison sentence of one year, probation, and ordered to undergo 200 hours of [[community service]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.courttv.com/people/2007/1207/pacman_jones_ap.html|title=Suspended NFL star 'Pacman' Jones pleads guilty in Las Vegas strip club melee|publisher=Court TV|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080608005654/http://www.courttv.com/people/2007/1207/pacman_jones_ap.html|archive-date=June 8, 2008|url-status=dead|access-date=October 14, 2008}}</ref>

On June 25, 2007, Tommy Urbanski and his wife, Kathy, sued Jones in civil court, claiming that Jones had bitten his left ankle and was responsible for the shooting.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://sports.yahoo.com/nfl/news?slug=ap-pacmancharges&prov=ap&type=lgns|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070628220438/http://sports.yahoo.com/nfl/news?slug=ap-pacmancharges&prov=ap&type=lgns|url-status=dead|archive-date=June 28, 2007|title=Yahoo! Sports – Sports News, Scores, Rumors, Fantasy Games, and more|publisher=Sports.yahoo.com|access-date=October 14, 2008}}</ref> The lawsuit also named the Tennessee Titans and the NFL as defendants, on the grounds that Jones' employers knew of his erratic behavior prior to the Minxx incident, but did not suspend him until afterward. Had the Titans suspended Jones prior to the NBA All-Star game, the suit still debated, and Jones would not have been invited to the Las Vegas events, and the incident would not have taken place.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.reviewjournal.com/news/nfl-team-tries-to-quash-lawsuit-by-paralyzed-man/|title=NFL team tries to quash lawsuit by paralyzed man|date=January 6, 2008 |publisher=Las Vegas Review Journal|access-date=November 16, 2021}}</ref>

On April 21, 2008, a document revealed that Jones, through intermediaries, paid $15,000 extortion money in two installments to Arvin Kenti Edwards, the alleged Minxx club shooter.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=3357972 |title=Police say Pacman paid 'extortion' cash in Vegas shooting|date=April 22, 2008 |publisher=ESPN |access-date=November 16, 2021| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20081016054433/http://sports.espn.go.com/nfl/news/story?id=3357972| archive-date= October 16, 2008 | url-status= live}}</ref>

On January 15, 2012, a jury ordered Jones to pay $11.6 million to Urbanski and Aaron Cudworth, a bouncer who was wounded, for Jones' role in the 2007 Las Vegas shooting. Jones' attorney said he planned to appeal the verdict.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2012-06-15 |title=Pacman forced to pay $11M to shooting victims |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/8058700/jury-orders-adam-pacman-jones-pay-11-million-shooting-victims |access-date=2025-04-05 |website=ESPN |agency=Associated Press}}</ref>

On January 9, 2015, the Nevada Supreme Court upheld the order for Jones to pay $11 million to Urbanski and $1.3 million to Cudworth.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/12142921/adam-pacman-jones-cincinnati-bengals-loses-124m-judgment-appeal-nevada|title=Adam Jones loses $12.4M appeal|date=January 9, 2015|website=[[ESPN]] NFL|agency=[[Associated Press]]}}</ref>

===2007–present===
On May 7, 2007, Jones was stopped at 12:45 a.m. on [[Interstate 65]] heading into downtown Nashville after an officer clocked him on radar at 79 miles per hour in a 55 miles per hour zone. Jones was driving the red 2004 [[Cadillac XLR]] Roadster which had been seized in the April 2006 cocaine bust, and which he had bought back from the police at auction.<ref name="red-cadillac" />

On June 18, 2007, Jones was sought by police for questioning after a shooting at an Atlanta strip club allegedly involving members of his entourage. According to police at the scene, Jones was not present during the shooting, and was not being charged.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=2908112 |title=Cops want to talk to Pacman about alleged shooting by entourage |publisher=ESPM |agency=Associated Press |access-date=October 14, 2008| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20080923224421/http://sports.espn.go.com/nfl/news/story?id=2908112| archive-date= September 23, 2008 | url-status= live}}</ref>

On August 13, 2007, regarding the February Las Vegas strip club incident, Jones told [[Bryant Gumbel]] of [[HBO|HBO Sports']] ''[[Real Sports with Bryant Gumbel]]''  he was innocent and had never hit the stripper or told anyone he was going to kill them. When asked about friend and convicted drug dealer Darryl Moore, Jones said that he did not know Moore was a drug dealer and felt surprised and betrayed. Jones also said he did not think he got a fair say in his April meeting with NFL commissioner [[Roger Goodell]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Pacman proclaims innocence in shooting |url=https://www.thestar.com/sports/football/2007/08/14/pacman_proclaims_innocence_in_shooting.html |website=The Toronto Star |access-date=November 16, 2021 |date=August 14, 2007}}</ref>

On January 15, 2008, Jones was accused of hitting a woman in a strip club in [[Atlanta]], [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]] on the morning of January 3. The woman, Wanda S. Jackson, was seeking an arrest warrant.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=3197653|title=Woman accuses Pacman of punching woman in club|date=January 15, 2008 |publisher=ESPN|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080926045759/http://sports.espn.go.com/nfl/news/story?id=3197653|archive-date=September 26, 2008|url-status=live|access-date=November 16, 2021}}</ref>

On June 21, 2008, the Associated Press reported Jones' $1.5 million home was in [[foreclosure]]. The home and {{convert|30|acre|ha}}, located in a Nashville suburb, was sold June 27 on the steps of the Williamson County Courthouse.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://nbcsports.msnbc.com/id/25287815/ |title=Home of 'Pacman' Jones up for foreclosure sale |publisher=NBS Sports |access-date=October 13, 2008 |date=June 20, 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120618042430/http://nbcsports.msnbc.com/id/25287815/ |archive-date=June 18, 2012 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Soon after, Jones decided he only wanted to be known as "Adam Jones" or "Mr. Jones," in an attempt to separate himself from his troubled past.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://sports.aol.com/story/_a/no-more-pacman-jones-wants-to-drop/n20080622124609990013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180612162105/http://sports.aol.com/story/_a/no-more-pacman-jones-wants-to-drop/n20080622124609990013 |url-status=dead |archive-date=June 12, 2018 |title=No more Pacman? Jones wants to drop nickname |publisher=AOL Sports |date=June 22, 2008 |access-date=June 23, 2008 }}</ref>

On October 8, 2008, Jones was involved in an altercation with his bodyguard in a Dallas hotel.<ref name="fight">{{cite web|url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=3633432 |title=Cowboys' Pacman gets in fight with bodyguard at Dallas hotel – NFL |publisher=ESPN |date=October 9, 2008 |access-date=December 29, 2010}}</ref> Although there was no police report, nor was anyone arrested or charged,<ref name="fight" /> Jones was suspended for a minimum of four games by the NFL for violating the league's personal conduct policy.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.patriots.com/news/nfl-suspends-cowboys-cb-jones-for-a-minimum-of-four-games-105241 |title=NFL suspends Cowboys CB Jones for a minimum of four games |work=New England Patriots |access-date=November 16, 2021| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20081017182747/http://www.nfl.com/news/story?id=09000d5d80ba4088&template=without-video&confirm=true| archive-date= October 17, 2008 | url-status= live}}</ref> On October 16, Jones entered an alcohol rehabilitation center.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.fantasysp.com/player/nfl/Adam_Jones/106042 |title=Adam Jones portal |publisher=Fantasysp.com |access-date=May 1, 2009}}</ref>

In a letter to Jones, Goodell called the Dallas incident the continuation of "a disturbing pattern of behavior and clearly inconsistent with the conditions I set for your continued participation in the NFL."

On January 3, 2017, Jones was arrested in Cincinnati's central district for obstructing official business, disorderly conduct, assault, and a felony charge of harassment with a bodily substance.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nfl.com/news/story/0ap3000000768799/article/adam-jones-arrested-on-harassment-assault-charges|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170104001027/http://www.nfl.com/news/story/0ap3000000768799/article/adam-jones-arrested-on-harassment-assault-charges|url-status=dead|archive-date=January 4, 2017| title=Adam Jones arrested on harassment, assault charges| access-date=January 3, 2017| website=NFL.com| first=Conor| last=Orr| date=January 3, 2017}}</ref> On May 15, 2017, Jones accepted a plea agreement, pleading guilty to one count of obstructing a police officer.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/19395044/adam-pacman-jones-cincinnati-bengals-pleads-guilty-apologizes-behavior|title=Pacman pleads guilty, apologizes for behavior|date=May 16, 2017 }}</ref> He received credit for time served (two days).<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.cincinnati.com/story/news/2017/05/16/adam-pacman-jones-pleads-obstructing-police/324744001/|title=Adam 'Pacman' Jones pleads, police release full arrest video}}</ref> Jones received a one-game suspension from the NFL on July 21, 2017, regarding the incident.<ref name="2017suspension" />

On July 10, 2018, Jones was attacked by an Atlanta airport employee, who was later arrested for assault.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cincinnati.com/story/sports/nfl/bengals/2018/07/11/video-shows-adam-jones-attacked-fighting-atlanta-airport/775171002/| title=Video shows ex-Cincinnati Bengals corner Adam Jones attacked, fighting at Atlanta airport| access-date=September 25, 2018| website=cincinnati.com| first=Paul Jr. |last=Dehner| date=July 11, 2018}}</ref> In February 2019, Jones was arrested for illegal bets in a casino, at a blackjack table. Footage of the incident was broadcast by TMZ and is currently available on [[YouTube]].
On February 15, 2021, Jones was arrested in [[Hamilton County, Ohio]], for misdemeanor assault.<ref>{{cite news |author=Alper, Josh |title=Adam "Pacman" Jones arrested, charged with misdemeanor assault |url=https://profootballtalk.nbcsports.com/2021/02/15/adam-pacman-jones-arrested-charged-with-misdemeanor-assault/ |website=NBCSports.com |date=February 15, 2021 |access-date=March 8, 2021}}</ref>

On September 11, 2023, Jones was arrested after police responded to a report of an unruly passenger at Cincinnati/Northern Kentucky International Airport. Jones was booked on misdemeanor counts of alcohol intoxication, disorderly conduct and terroristic threatening. He was later released.<ref>{{cite news |agency=Associated Press |title=Ex-NFL DB Adam 'Pacman' Jones arrested at Cincinnati airport |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/38378858/pacman-jones-arrested-cincinnati-airport |website=ESPN.com |date=September 11, 2023 |access-date=September 11, 2023}}</ref>

On November 15, 2024, Jones was arrested at [[AT&T Stadium]] in [[Arlington, Texas]] and booked into Tarrant County Jail on multiple charges after getting into a fight at the stadium's bar area following the [[Jake Paul vs Mike Tyson]] bout. Jones was charged with one count of assault on a peace officer, one count of public intoxication, one count of evading and one count of resisting arrest.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/5926230/2024/11/16/adam-pacman-arrested-mike-tyson-jake-paul-fight-arlington/|title=Former NFL player Adam 'Pacman' Jones arrested on multiple charges after Mike Tyson-Jake Paul fight, police say|first=Lauren|last=Merola|publisher=The Athletic|date=November 16, 2024|accessdate=November 16, 2024}}</ref>

On June 7, 2025, Jones was arrested near Cincinnati and charged with public intoxication, disorderly conduct, and assault of an officer. He was booked into the Kenton County Jail in northern Kentucky shortly before 2 a.m. and released later that day on a $100,000 bond. A court appearance was scheduled for the following Monday.<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/6410476/2025/06/07/adam-pacman-jones-arrest-kentucky/ | title=Adam 'Pacman' Jones arrested, charged with assaulting officer, public intoxication | work=[[The New York Times]] | date=June 7, 2025 | accessdate=7 June 2025 | author=Puleo, Mark}}</ref>

'''Adam Hartford Seward''' (born June 15, 1982) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[linebacker]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He was selected by the [[Carolina Panthers]] in the fifth round of the [[2005 NFL draft]] after playing [[college football]] for the [[UNLV Rebels football|UNLV Rebels]]. Along with being a player for the Panthers, he also played for the [[Indianapolis Colts]] and [[Jacksonville Jaguars]].

==Early life==
Adam Hartford Seward was born on June 15, 1982, at Carle Clinic Hospital in [[Champaign-Urbana, Illinois]]. Seward attended [[Bonanza High School]] in Las Vegas, NV. He was a two-time All-State selection at linebacker and a starting running back. His biggest game came during his senior season at national powerhouse [[Bishop Gorman High School]]. Seward rushed for over 200 yards and two touchdowns, leading the Bengals, who were big underdogs, to an overtime victory over the Gaels. The game is currently Bonanza's last victory over Bishop Gorman in football.

In addition to football, he was a star athlete in track ([[shot put]] and [[discus]]), and won the Nevada state heavyweight title in [[sport wrestling|wrestling]]. He and former [[Ultimate Fighting Championship|UFC]] heavyweight champion [[Frank Mir]], who were teammates in 1998, are among the 12 state wrestling champions in Bonanza High School's history.

==College career==
Known as one of the top defensive players in the State of Nevada during his senior year, Seward opted to stay home and signed a scholarship offer to attend college in his hometown at the [[University of Nevada, Las Vegas]], where he played four years for the Rebels. He became a starter during his freshman season and went on to be named All-[[Mountain West Conference]] three times.  When he graduated in 2004, he left as both UNLV's and the [[Mountain West Conference]]'s all-time leader in tackles (Though his UNLV record still stands, [[New Mexico]]'s [[Carmen Messina]] would go on to break his MWC record during his final game of the 2011 season).  He also had six [[quarterback sack|sacks]], six forced [[fumble]]s, four fumble recoveries, and two [[interception]]s. Seward was also an active member of the [[Sigma Alpha Epsilon]] fraternity.{{Cn|date=September 2025}}

==Professional career==
At the 2005 NFL combine, Seward (248 lbs.) was clocked at 4.56 in the 40-yard dash, leading many NFL scouts to believe that he would be a late second to early third round pick. However, scouts soon discovered a broken bone in his right foot, which caused his draft stock to fall dramatically. Nevertheless, Seward was selected by the [[Carolina Panthers]] in the fifth round (149th overall) of the [[2005 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=2005 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2005/draft.htm |access-date=2023-05-07 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> Seward rapidly became a star special teams player and back-up linebacker during his rookie season. Over the course of his career with the Panthers, he was frequently known as one of Carolina's best special teams players.{{citation needed|date=November 2019}} He also served as a backup to All-Pro linebackers [[Dan Morgan]] and [[Jon Beason]]. In 2008, with one of the best defenses in the NFL, Carolina compiled a record of 12–4 and won the [[NFC South]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=2008 Carolina Panthers Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/car/2008.htm |access-date=2025-06-22 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref>

After a successful four-year stint with the Panthers that include two playoff runs and a trip to the 2005 NFC Championship Game, Seward signed with the Indianapolis Colts as an [[Unrestricted Free Agent]].<ref>{{cite web | title=Colts sign former Panthers LB Seward, waive RB Dawson | website=NFL.com | date=2009-03-24 | url=https://www.nfl.com/news/colts-sign-former-panthers-lb-seward-waive-rb-dawson-09000d5d80f6bee1 | access-date=2025-06-22}}</ref> Though released during the 2009 preseason, Seward would sign with the [[Jacksonville Jaguars]] the next day.<ref>{{cite web | last=Kuharsky | first=Paul | title=Seward stays in division, joins Jags | website=ESPN.com | date=2009-08-24 | url=https://www.espn.com/blog/afcsouth/post/_/id/2368/seward-stays-in-division-joins-jags | access-date=2025-06-22}}</ref> He spent the 2009–10 season as a member of the Jaguars.

==Life after football==
In 2010, after undergoing surgery to repair a [[sports hernia]] that required intensive repairs to not only the abdominal area, but also to several tendons in the right leg, Seward retired from the NFL and took a job with the NFL's representative office in [[Mexico City]]. He also hosted a Spanish-language radio show in Mexico City aimed at promoting football in Latin America. In 2011, he received two top-level Spanish-language certifications from [[Universidad Nacional Autonoma de Mexico]].

After achieving success in Mexico, Seward was employed by the NFL's representative office in Beijing, China. In 2012, he served as a Chinese-language analyst for NFL football in China on Sina-Weibo.

In 2014, Seward was named the defensive coordinator of the Kyoto University football team in Kyoto, Japan.

Currently,{{when|date=November 2019}} Seward serves as the president of Goober Foundation Properties, Ltd., a real estate investment, management, and development firm. The company specializes in multi-family properties and land development with operations in four states.

==Personal life==
Seward holds a master's degree in business administration from the [[University of Southern California]]. He is fluent in Spanish, Chinese, and Japanese.

His father, Tom, played for [[Eastern Illinois University]], and was the co-captain of the squad which won the [[NCAA Division II]] football title in 1978.  He later was an assistant coach for The University of Illinois, [[Howard University]], University of Nevada Las Vegas, and Southern Illinois University. Seward's mother, Amy, was a [[cheerleader]] for the Chicago Bears.

His younger brother, Mark, played college football for the University of Nevada, Las Vegas.

==Legal problems==
On March 16, 2021, was arrested for leaving the scene of an accident. A female passenger sustained serious injuries. On April 26, 2023, Seward was found guilty for his role in the incident two years prior, a hit and run crash that left the woman injured. In the aftermath, Seward received a year of probation and a 24–60 month suspended prison sentence. He was also ordered to complete a controlled substance abuse evaluation and submit to random testing. He also could not consume any alcoholic substances during the time of his probation.

'''Adam Richard Snyder''' (born January 30, 1982) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was an [[offensive guard]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He was selected in the third round in the [[2005 NFL draft]] by the [[San Francisco 49ers]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=2005 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2005/draft.htm |access-date=2023-05-07 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> He also played for the [[Arizona Cardinals]] and the [[New York Giants]].

At the [[University of Oregon]] he was the winner of the [[Morris Trophy]], and played every position but center. His junior and senior seasons he was considered one of the premier left [[offensive tackle]]s in college football.

==Early life==
Adam Snyder attended [[La Serna High School]] in [[Whittier, California]], where he played football. He was coached by Ken LaVigne from 1999 to 2000.

==College career==
Snyder was redshirted in 2000 at Oregon and saw action in the final 11 games of the 2001 season, when he served as the for the year.

Snyder departed as one of Oregon's most decorated linemen of all time, becoming the Ducks' third [[Morris Trophy]] recipient (as the Pac-10 Conference's top lineman) ever. The three-year starter and the school's first two-time first-team all-league offensive line stalwart in four decades extended his string of career starting assignments to 35 at three different positions while playing in 48 of 49 outings.

'''Adam S. Terry''' (born September 1, 1982) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was an [[offensive tackle]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Syracuse Orange football|Syracuse Orange]] and was selected by the [[Baltimore Ravens]] in the second round of the [[2005 NFL draft]].

He was also a member of the [[Indianapolis Colts]], [[San Diego Chargers]], [[Jacksonville Jaguars]] and [[Tennessee Titans]].

==Early life==
Terry attended Queensbury High School in [[Queensbury, New York|Queensbury]], [[New York (state)|New York]]. As a junior, he was a first-team All-Conference pick and a first-team All-State selection, and was named an All-East selection by Prep Football Report.

==College career==
Terry played [[college football]] at [[Syracuse University]], where he started in the final 35 games of his career there. He earned a degree in history.

==Professional career==
===Baltimore Ravens===
[[File:EndRavensSteelersGame.jpg|thumb|left|250px|Terry (78) with the Ravens in 2006.]]
Terry was selected by the [[Baltimore Ravens]] in the second round (64th overall) in the [[2005 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=2005 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2005/draft.htm |access-date=2023-05-07 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> In his rookie season, he played in seven games.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Adam Terry 2005 Game Log |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/T/TerrAd20/gamelog/2005/ |access-date=2025-06-22 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> In the 2006 season he played in all 16 regular season games and was part of an offensive line that only allowed 17 sacks, a franchise record. Furthermore, that season the Ravens rushed for 1,637 yards and 11 touchdowns. However, Terry continued to struggle with injuries, which led to his departure.

===Indianapolis Colts===
Terry signed with the [[Indianapolis Colts]] on March 12, 2010.
Terry was cut by Colts following Training Camp.

===San Diego Chargers===
Signed on September 5, 2010, following his release from the Colts, Terry spent two games in San Diego before being released to make room for receiver [[Kelley Washington]] on November 4.

===Tennessee Titans===
On August 15, 2011, he signed with the [[Tennessee Titans]], but he was released by the team on September 3, 2011.<ref>{{Citation |date=December 30, 2011 |title=NFL Transactions Report |url=http://www.nfl.com/transactions?transactionMonth=9&transactionYear=2011&transactionTeamAbbr=TEN&prevTransactionMonth=9&prevTransactionYear=2011&prevTransactionTeamAbbr=}}</ref>

Smith was selected by the Pittsburgh Steelers in the fourth round, 109th pick overall, of the [[1999 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1999 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1999/draft.htm |access-date=2023-03-29 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title= The Aaron Smith file|url= http://pittsburghlive.com/images/video/2008_pdfs/0802steelers.pdf|publisher= [[Pittsburgh Tribune-Review]]|date= August 2, 2008|access-date= August 26, 2008}}{{dead link|date=January 2018 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> Smith played in every Steelers' game at left defensive end from 2000 through 2006.<ref name=ESPNstats>{{cite web |url= https://www.espn.com/nfl/player/stats/_/id/1862/aaron-smith|title= Aaron Smith|access-date=August 26, 2008 |work= Stats|publisher= [[ESPN.com]]}}</ref> Smith has been considered an ideal defensive end in Pittsburgh's [[3-4 defense]].<ref>{{cite news |first= Michael|last= Smith|title= Defensive linemen do the dirty work in 3-4|url= https://www.espn.com/nfl/columns/story?id=1946758|work= [[ESPN.com]]|date= December 15, 2004|access-date=August 16, 2008}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |first= Ron|last= Cook|title= One man Steelers can't do without|url= http://www.post-gazette.com/pg/08238/906809-87.stm|publisher= [[Pittsburgh Post-Gazette]]|date= August 25, 2008|access-date=August 26, 2008| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20080828013427/http://www.post-gazette.com/pg/08238/906809-87.stm| archive-date= August 28, 2008 | url-status= live}}</ref> Smith won a [[Super Bowl ring]] with the Steelers in [[Super Bowl XL]], during the 2005 season. He recorded four tackles throughout the game.<ref name=SteelBio>{{cite web|url= http://news.steelers.com/team/player/49248/|title= Aaron Smith #91|access-date= December 25, 2009|publisher= Steelers.com|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20091231122033/http://news.steelers.com/team/player/49248/|archive-date= December 31, 2009|url-status= dead}}</ref>  After the 2008 season, Smith won another ring with the Steelers in [[Super Bowl XLIII]].

On February 27, 2007, the Steelers resigned Smith to a 5-year, [[United States dollar|US$]]25 million contract.<ref>{{cite news |first= Joe|last= Mandak|author-link= Associated Press|title= Steelers re-sign defensive end Aaron Smith|url= https://www.usatoday.com/sports/football/nfl/2007-02-28-2515274016_x.htm|publisher= [[USA Today]]|date= March 28, 2008|access-date=August 26, 2008}}</ref> Through the [[2007 NFL season|2007 season]], Smith ranks ninth all-time on the Steelers sacks list.<ref name=EagerLost/> After missing parts of three games with a knee injury early in the 2007 season, Smith missed the last four games due to a torn biceps muscle  while playing against the [[New England Patriots]] in early December. Smith made a full recovery from the injury and returned to his starting position in 2008, recording 44 tackles and 5.5 sacks.<ref name=EagerLost>{{cite news|first= Scott|last= Brown|title= Steelers' Smith eager to make up for lost time|url= http://www.pittsburghlive.com/x/pittsburghtrib/sports/steelers/s_580684.html?source=rss&feed=9|publisher= [[Pittsburgh Tribune-Review]]|date= August 2, 2008|access-date= August 2, 2008|url-status= dead|archive-url= https://archive.today/20130131160012/http://www.pittsburghlive.com/x/pittsburghtrib/sports/steelers/s_580684.html?source=rss&feed=9|archive-date= January 31, 2013}}</ref>

In 2009, Smith played in Pittsburgh's first five games before sustaining a torn [[rotator cuff]] in an Oct 10 win over the Detroit Lions. On Oct 14, the Steelers placed Smith on the [[injured reserve list]], ending his 2009 season.<ref name=bradrules>{{cite news |first= Ed|last= Bouchette|title= Aaron Smith out for season; Steelers sign rookie Harris |url= http://www.post-gazette.com/pg/09287/1005355-66.stm|publisher= [[Pittsburgh Post-Gazette]]|date= October 14, 2009|access-date=October 14, 2009| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20091016231536/http://www.post-gazette.com/pg/09287/1005355-66.stm| archive-date= October 16, 2009 | url-status= live}}</ref> He was hurt again in 2010, playing in only 6 games, replaced by [[Ziggy Hood]].  In 2011, he played in 4 games before being placed on the injured reserve list for a neck injury, marking the third time in three years that he had been placed on the injured reserve list.<ref name="Whoknows">{{cite news |date=October 22, 2011 |title=Aaron Smith placed on IR. |url=http://www.steelers.com/news/article-1/Aaron-Smith-placed-on-IR/d13a34f9-f7ff-4f08-ac4a-bbe552da576e |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111024073348/http://www.steelers.com/news/article-1/Aaron-Smith-placed-on-IR/d13a34f9-f7ff-4f08-ac4a-bbe552da576e |archive-date=October 24, 2011 |access-date=October 22, 2011 |publisher=[[Pittsburgh Steelers]] |df=mdy-all}}</ref><ref name=Whoknows1>{{cite news |first=Ed |last=Bouchette |title=Ed: Neck Injury, not Foot, Drove Smith to IR |url=http://plus.sites.post-gazette.com/index.php/pro-sports/steelers/112722-ed-neck-injury-not-foot-drove-smith-to-ir |publisher=[[Pittsburgh Post-Gazette]] |date=October 23, 2011 |access-date=October 23, 2011 |archive-date=October 29, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111029084645/http://plus.sites.post-gazette.com/index.php/pro-sports/steelers/112722-ed-neck-injury-not-foot-drove-smith-to-ir |url-status=dead }} <!-- Remove this comment when fixing the dead link: {{Cite web| url=http://plus.sites.post-gazette.com/index.php/pro-sports/steelers/112722-ed-neck-injury-not-foot-drove-smith-to-ir | title=Ed: Neck Injury, not Foot, Drove Smith to IR | accessdate=October 23, 2011 | url-status=dead | archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20111029084645/http://plus.sites.post-gazette.com/index.php/pro-sports/steelers/112722-ed-neck-injury-not-foot-drove-smith-to-ir | archivedate=October 29, 2011}}--></ref> He was released on March 2, 2012.

On August 3, 2012, during a ceremony in Latrobe, PA, Smith officially retired from the NFL.<ref>http://www.cbssports.com/nfl/blog/nfl-rapidreports/19719758/steelers-set-aaron-smiths-retirement-ceremony {{Dead link|date=February 2022}}</ref>

In 2017, Smith served as an assistant football & basketball coach at [[North Allegheny Senior High School]] in [[Wexford, Pennsylvania]].

On July 29, 2023, Smith was named to the Pittsburgh Steelers Hall of Honor.<ref>{{Cite web | title=Steelers announce Hall of Honor Class of 2023 | url=https://www.steelers.com/news/steelers-announce-hall-of-honor-class-of-2023 | access-date=2025-08-28 | website=www.steelers.com}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Smith and his wife, Jaimie, are devout [[Christians]] who first came to know [[Christ]] while Smith was on the Steelers. Smith has experienced great joy in following Christ, saying during an interview:<ref>{{cite web |title=Steelers' Defensive End: Aaron Smith|url=https://cbn.com/article/not-selected/steelers-defensive-end-aaron-smith-0|website=CBN.com|publisher=[[Christian Broadcasting Network]]|access-date=July 7, 2025}}</ref>

{{blockquote|The joy Christ gives me - I’m always happy. You can’t take my joy away. No matter what happens in life. We’re talking about your eternal salvation. We’re talking about spending the rest of your life, after you pass away, in heaven with the Lord. That’s the biggest decision you’ll ever make in your life. Life isn’t going to be perfect. But you’ll have someone to do it with you. You’re not doing it by yourself. Christ is right there with you the whole time. It’s the biggest thing you’ll ever do in your life. And it’s the greatest thing you’ll ever do, is to come to know and accept Jesus Christ as your Savior.}}

Smith has three brothers named David, Stephan, and Kevin.

Smith and his wife Jaimie have five children: daughters Elliana, Elysia, and Emilia and sons Ezekiel and Elijiah. His son Elijiah suffered from [[acute lymphoblastic leukemia]] but completed his treatments successfully and is now cancer-free.<ref>{{cite news| url=http://www.post-gazette.com/pg/08349/935071-87.stm | work=Pittsburgh Post-Gazette | title=Since October, the pain has had a new definition for a family of Aaron Smith | first=Ron | last=Cook | date=December 14, 2008}}</ref>

Smith was a consensus All-State selection at Sierra High School ([[Colorado Springs, Colorado|Colorado Springs]], Colo.), he also lettered in [[basketball]] and was a two-time All-Conference choice in both sports.

'''Aaron T. Shea''' (born December 5, 1976) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[tight end]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He was selected by the [[Cleveland Browns]] in the fourth round of the [[2000 NFL draft]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Michigan Wolverines football|Michigan Wolverines]].

Shea also played for the [[San Diego Chargers]].

==College career==
Shea attended the [[University of Michigan]] where he played [[fullback (American football)|fullback]] and tight end.

===Cleveland Browns===
He was selected by the [[Cleveland Browns]] in the fourth round (110th overall) of the [[2000 NFL draft]] and went on to play six seasons for Cleveland.<ref>{{Cite web |title=2000 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2000/draft.htm |access-date=2023-03-19 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> During his time there, he caught 97 passes for 851 yards and seven touchdowns. He fumbled only once in his career - during his rookie season in 2000.

===San Diego Chargers===
As a free agent in the 2006 offseason a handful of teams were reportedly interested in Shea, including the [[Houston Texans]], [[Pittsburgh Steelers]], [[San Diego Chargers]], [[San Francisco 49ers]] and [[Seattle Seahawks]]. On March 17, Shea signed a three-year contract with San Diego.<ref>{{cite news|title=Chargers sign TE Aaron Shea|url=https://www.chargers.com/news/2006/03/17/chargers-sign-te-aaron-shea|access-date=October 7, 2016|work=NFL.com|date=March 17, 2006}}{{Dead link|date=September 2018 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> A back injury bothered him throughout the preseason and forced him to miss the team's first three regular season contests. On September 26, he was placed on season-ending injured reserve.

Shea was released after just one season in San Diego on March 2, 2007.

==Retirement==
In June 2007, ''[[The Plain Dealer]]'' reported Shea was receiving interest from his former team, the Cleveland Browns. However, Shea remained unsigned as the 2007 season began.

In May 2008, Shea officially retired from the NFL.

He worked for the Browns from 2011 to 2014,<ref>{{cite news|last1=Cabot|first1=Mary Kay|title=Cleveland Browns hire former TE Aaron Shea for front office post|url=http://www.cleveland.com/browns/index.ssf/2011/07/cleveland_browns_hire_former_t.html|access-date=October 7, 2016|work=The Plain Dealer|date=July 20, 2011}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last1=Reed|first1=Tom|title=Cleveland Browns part ways with player engagement director Aaron Shea|url=http://www.cleveland.com/browns/index.ssf/2014/03/cleveland_browns_part_ways_wit_3.html|access-date=October 7, 2016|work=The Plain Dealer|date=March 7, 2014}}</ref> and later became an insurance agent.<ref>{{cite news|last1=O'Connor|first1=Ian|title='Now you've pissed off the GOAT.' An 'angry' Tom Brady returns|url=http://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/page/HotReadx161007/new-england-patriots-qb-tom-brady-for-blood-week-5-game-cleveland-browns|access-date=October 7, 2016|work=ESPN.com|date=October 7, 2016}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Shea married the former Caitlin Gibbons in Cleveland on June 21, 2003. They have two daughters, Cadence and Ireland and one son Kinzy.

Shea and his family were involved in a minor car accident on [[New York State Route 430|Route 430]] in the town of [[Ellery, New York|Ellery]], New York, near [[Chautauqua Lake]] on July 6, 2010. All five members of the Shea family escaped injury.<ref>{{cite news |author= Rizzuto, Robert|title= Ellery Accident |url= http://www.post-journal.com/page/content.detail/id/561735.html |publisher= [[The Post-Journal]] |date= July 7, 2010}}</ref>

[[Wisconsin Badgers football|Wisconsin]] | undraftedyear = 1999 | pastteams = * [[Chicago Bears]] ({{NFL Year|1999}})* * [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]] ({{NFL Year|1999}}–{{NFL Year|2003}}) * [[New Orleans Saints]] ({{NFL Year|2004}}–{{NFL Year|2008}}) * [[Atlanta Falcons]] ({{NFL Year|2009}}) | highlights = * [[Super Bowl champion]] ([[Super Bowl XXXVII|XXXVII]]) * [[NFL Europe]] Offensive [[Most Valuable Player|MVP]] (2000) | statlabel1 = [[Carry (American football)|Rushing attempts]] | statvalue1 = 386 | statlabel2 = [[Rushing yards]] | statvalue2 = 1,526 | statlabel3 = [[Reception (American football)|Receptions]] | statvalue3 = 166 | statlabel4 = [[Receiving yards]] | statvalue4 = 1,175 | statlabel5 = [[Return yards]] | statvalue5 = 3,934 | statlabel6 = [[Touchdown|Total touchdowns]] | statvalue6 = 12 }} '''Aaron Stecker''' (born November 13, 1975) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[running back]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Western Illinois Leathernecks football|Western Illinois Leathernecks]] and [[Wisconsin Badgers football|Wisconsin Badgers]]. He was signed by the [[Chicago Bears]] as an [[undrafted free agent]] in 1999. Stecker also played for the [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]], [[New Orleans Saints]], and [[Atlanta Falcons]]. He earned a [[Super Bowl ring]] with the Buccaneers in [[Super Bowl XXXVII]]. Mainly used as a backup for most of his career, Stecker started 14 games during his five years with the Saints, and also often served as a [[kick returner]] for both Tampa Bay and New Orleans. On April 20, 2010, Stecker announced that he was retiring from football,Tom Ziemer, [http://host.madison.com/sports/football/article_67e95cbe-490a-11df-8c4b-001cc4c03286.html "NFL: Stecker retires after 11-year run"], [[Wisconsin State Journal|Madison.com]], April 15, 2010. although later in 2010, he worked out for, but did not sign with, the [[Green Bay Packers]].Greg Bedard, [http://www.jsonline.com/sports/packers/104915279.html "Packers' Jennings vents frustrations"], ''[[Milwaukee Journal-Sentinel]]'', October 13, 2010. ==Early life== Stecker attended [[Ashwaubenon High School]] in [[Ashwaubenon, Wisconsin]], and was a [[Letterman (sports)|letterman]] in football and [[baseball]]. He led the Ashwaubenon football team to the state championship game in 1993. His number, 27, has been retired. ==College career== Stecker began his [[College football|college career]] at [[Wisconsin Badgers football|Wisconsin]] in 1995. He spent two years with the University of Wisconsin, recording three 100-yard games, a 100-yard kick return for a [[touchdown]], and a 63-yard [[punt return]] for a touchdown. In 1997, he transferred to [[Western Illinois University|Western Illinois]] after the emergence of future [[Heisman Trophy]] winner [[Ron Dayne]] pushed Stecker from his starting role with the Badgers.{{Cite web|url=http://www.sptimes.com/News/052300/Sports/Stecker_s_trek_may_en.shtml|title=Sports: Stecker's trek may end at NFL|website=www.sptimes.com|access-date=January 28, 2017}} During the 1997 season, Stecker recorded 2,293 rushing yards en route to winning the [[Gateway Football Conference]] player of the year award. Stecker finished his career at Western Illinois as the school's all-time leading rusher, with 3,799 yards in just two seasons. This record was broken by Travis Glasford in 2005, and is now held by Herb Donaldson, as of 2008. == Professional career == {{NFL predraft | height ft = 5 | height in = 9 1/2 | weight = 210 | dash = 4.82 | ten split = 1.74 | twenty split = 2.83 | shuttle = 4.17 | cone drill = 7.00 | vertical = 32.5 | broad ft = 9 | broad in = 5 | bench = 23 | arm span = 29 1/4 | hand span = 9 1/2 | note = All values from [[NFL Combine]]{{Cite web |url=https://draftscout.com/dsprofile.php?PlayerId=1754&DraftYear=1999 |title=1999 Draft Scout Aaron Stecker, Western Illinois NFL Draft Scout College Football Profile |access-date=March 20, 2023 |website=draftscout.com}}{{Cite web |url=https://nflcombineresults.com/playerpage.php?i=5162 |title=Aaron Stecker, Combine Results, RB - Western Illinois |website=nflcombineresults.com |access-date=March 20, 2023}} }} === Chicago Bears === Stecker spent the 1999 training camp with the [[Chicago Bears]]; however, he did not make the active roster.{{Cite news|url=http://host.madison.com/sports/football/nfl-stecker-retires-after--year-run/article_67e95cbe-490a-11df-8c4b-001cc4c03286.html|title=NFL: Stecker retires after 11-year run|author=Tom Ziemer|newspaper=madison.com|language=en|access-date=January 27, 2017}} === Scottish Claymores === Before the 2000 season, the [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]] allocated Stecker to the [[Scottish Claymores]] of [[NFL Europe]]. Stecker led the league in total scrimmage yards through the first two weeks in the season.{{Cite news|url=http://nfl.packers.com/news/releases/2000/04/04-27.html|title=Packers.com {{!}} Press Releases {{!}} April 27, 2000|access-date=January 27, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170202033540/http://nfl.packers.com/news/releases/2000/04/04-27.html|archive-date=February 2, 2017|url-status=dead}} He wound up garnering Offensive MVP honors.{{Cite web|url=http://www.esspeedee.com/claymores/claymores.php|title=About the Scottish Claymores / Team Records and History - Scottish Claymores|website=www.esspeedee.com|access-date=January 27, 2017}} === Tampa Bay Buccaneers === Early in his career in Tampa Bay, Stecker credits [[Fred McAfee]] for bolstering his confidence.{{Cite news|url=http://archive.jsonline.com/sports/92373494.html|title=Former Badger Aaron Stecker had long career despite being undrafted|language=en|access-date=January 27, 2017}} During the 2000 season, Stecker began returning kickoffs for the Bucs.{{Cite web|url=http://www.espn.com/nfl/player/stats/_/id/2401/aaron-stecker|title=Aaron Stecker|website=ESPN.com|access-date=January 27, 2017}} During his four years with the team, he became a core special teams player, along with sporadic duty as a pass-catching back.{{Cite web|url=http://www.nfl.com/player/aaronstecker/2503119/careerstats|title=Aaron Stecker: Career Stats at NFL.com|website=www.nfl.com|language=en|access-date=January 27, 2017}} He also won [[Super Bowl XXXVII]] with the team before leaving after 2003. === New Orleans Saints === Signing with the [[New Orleans Saints]] before 2004, Stecker became a return man and scat back. Competing with established backs such as [[Reggie Bush]] and [[Deuce McAllister]] led to sparse playing time.{{Cite news|url=http://www.espn.com/espn/wire/_/section/nfl/id/2953049|title=Being on the bubble is old hat for Stecker|newspaper=ESPN.com|access-date=January 28, 2017}} He was placed on injured reserve during the 2008 season and did not return to the team the following year.{{Cite web|url=http://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=3712893|title=Hamstring lands Saints' Stecker on injured reserve|date=November 19, 2008|website=ESPN.com|access-date=January 27, 2017}}{{Cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/S/StecAa00.htm|title=Aaron Stecker Stats {{!}} Pro-Football-Reference.com|website=Pro-Football-Reference.com|language=en|access-date=January 27, 2017}} === Atlanta Falcons === Stecker was signed by the [[Atlanta Falcons]] in the middle the 2009 season, where he played mostly on special teams. He carried the ball five times and caught it five times as well.{{Cite web|url=http://football-players.pointafter.com/l/19666/Aaron-Stecker|title=Aaron Stecker|website=football-players.pointafter.com|language=en-us|access-date=January 28, 2017}}{{Dead link|date=September 2018 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} The Packers also showed interest in Stecker in 2009.{{Cite web|url=http://www.totalpackers.com/2009/10/packers-tried-to-bring-in-aaron-stecker/|title=Packers Tried to Bring In Aaron Stecker|website=www.totalpackers.com|date=October 26, 2009 |language=en-US|access-date=January 28, 2017}} === Retirement === In April 2010, Stecker retired. '''Adalius Donquail Thomas''' ({{IPAc-en|ə|ˈ|d|eɪ|l|ə|s}}; born July 18, 1977) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[linebacker]] for ten seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL).  He played [[college football]] for the [[Southern Miss Golden Eagles football|Southern Miss Golden Eagles]].  He was selected by the [[Baltimore Ravens]] in the sixth round of the [[2000 NFL draft]], and also played for the NFL's [[New England Patriots]].

==Early life==
Thomas attended Central Coosa High School in [[Rockford, Alabama]], and was a letterman in football and basketball. In football, as a senior, he was named as a Class 4A all-state selection by the ''[[Birmingham News]]'' and as an honorable mention Class 4A all-state selection by the ''[[Montgomery Advertiser]]''. In basketball, as a senior, he led his team to the State Title and was named the Alabama Class 4A Player of the Year.{{citation needed|date=August 2021}}

==College career==
Thomas attended the [[University of Southern Mississippi]], where he was a star defensive end for coach [[Jeff Bower (American football)|Jeff Bower]]'s [[Southern Miss Golden Eagles football]] team. Thomas led one of the top defenses in college football, notching [[Conference USA]] Defensive Player of the Year honors his junior and senior years. The Golden Eagles won three Conference USA championships (1996, 1997, and 1999) in his four years in Hattiesburg, losing only two conference games and winning two Liberty Bowls.

Thomas was named a Freshman [[All-American]] by the [[Sporting News]] in 1996, leading the Golden Eagles to an 8–3 record and a share of the Conference USA title. Southern Miss finished 9–3 in Thomas's sophomore season, en route to a Conference USA Championship and a victory in the [[Liberty Bowl]]. Thomas was named to the All-Conference first-team.

Statistically speaking, Thomas's best season came in 1998, when he tallied 71 tackles, in addition to a conference-high 12.5 sacks and 20 tackles-for-loss. Thomas was named a first-team All-American and tied for Defensive Player of the Year. Thomas earned third-team All-American and  Defensive Player of the Year honors as a senior, in addition to being named the MVP of the 1999 [[Liberty Bowl]]. He was also named as a finalist for the [[Conerly Trophy]].

Thomas was also a power forward on the Golden Eagles basketball team in the 1995–96 and 1996–97 seasons, making him the first player in USM history to play both football and basketball.{{citation needed|date=August 2021}}

===Baltimore Ravens===
Thomas was drafted by the [[Baltimore Ravens]] in the sixth round (186th overall) in the [[2000 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=2000 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2000/draft.htm |access-date=2023-03-19 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> Competing with [[Peter Boulware]] and [[Michael McCrary]] for playing time, Thomas made only 89 tackles in his first three years. He was inactive for 12 games in his rookie season, but played in all 16 games in the 2001 season, starting two at defensive end. In 2002, he started 12 games at defensive end, recording two interceptions as well as 15 special teams tackles. In 2003, Thomas was recognized for his special teams play and was selected to his first [[Pro Bowl]]. That year, he registered 34 tackles, 8 passes defended, 4 sacks, and a forced fumble. He was placed on [[injured reserve]] by the Ravens on December 17, but still led the team with 23 special teams tackles.

In 2004, Thomas started all 16 games for the first time in his career. While still collecting 16 special teams tackles, he amassed 72 tackles, 4 forced fumbles, 5 passes defended, an interception and 8 sacks. In 2005, with Boulware relegated to situational pass-rush duty, Thomas was named the starting outside linebacker, where he accumulated 84 total tackles and 9 sacks. He also saw limited time at [[cornerback]] during that season.{{citation needed|date=January 2025}} He had two interceptions on the year and three forced fumbles; he returned three turnovers for touchdowns, making him the NFL's leader in non-offensive touchdowns that season.

Thomas earned his second Pro Bowl bid in 2006 as part of a Ravens defense that finished first in the league en route to a 13–3 record. He was a first-team [[All-Pro]] after setting a career-high with 106 tackles and 11 sacks, as well as notching 1 interception, 1 safety, 7 passes defensed, and 1 fumble recovery returned 57 yards for a touchdown. It proved to be, without a doubt, his finest season as a pro.{{citation needed|date=August 2021}}

===New England Patriots===
On March 3, 2007, Thomas signed a 5-year contract with the [[New England Patriots]] worth $35 million, including $20 million in guaranteed money. After the move, Patriots head coach [[Bill Belichick]] told Thomas that he had "backed up the [[The Brink's Company|Brink's]] truck" to pay him.<ref name="ESPN">{{cite web|url=https://www.espn.com/boston/columns/story?id=4730078|title=Will Belichick's message be heeded?|work=ESPNBoston.com|first=Mike|last=Reiss|date=2009-12-10|access-date=2009-12-22}}</ref> Thomas played mainly at inside linebacker in the Patriots' 3-4 defense in [[2007 New England Patriots season|2007]], rotating with veterans [[Tedy Bruschi]] and [[Junior Seau]]. As the Patriots progressed through an undefeated 2007 regular season, Thomas handed out "humble pie" T-shirts to his teammates in the locker room, echoing's Belichick's message of staying humble after each win.<ref name="ESPN" /> After a season-ending injury to outside linebacker [[Rosevelt Colvin]] in late November, Thomas started the remainder of the season and eventually [[Super Bowl XLII]] at outside linebacker. In that game, Thomas had a postseason-high two sacks and a forced fumble.

Thomas continued to start at outside linebacker for the Patriots in [[2008 New England Patriots season|2008]]. He led the team with five sacks until suffering a season-ending arm injury in Week 10 against the [[Buffalo Bills]]. He was placed on injured reserve on December 5.

In [[2009 New England Patriots season|2009]], Thomas began the season on the active list; however, he was deactivated for the October 18 game against the [[Tennessee Titans]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.espn.com/boston/nfl/news/story?id=4582424|title=Patriots LB Adalius Thomas discusses his recent deactivation|work=[[ESPN.com]]|first=Mike|last=Reiss|date=2009-10-21|access-date=2009-10-21| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20091024114612/http://sports.espn.go.com/boston/nfl/news/story?id=4582424| archive-date= 24 October 2009 | url-status= live}}</ref> Recording one sack on the season to that point, Thomas was asked by the press if he used the decision by Belichick as motivation to perform better. He responded "I don't need something like this to fire me up. This isn't [[kindergarten]]. I don't play [those] games."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.espn.com/boston/nfl/news/story?id=4582424|title=Thomas addresses recent deactivation|work=ESPNBoston.com|first=Mike|last=Reiss|date=2009-10-21|access-date=2009-12-22}}</ref>

Thomas was one of four Patriots sent home as a result of being late for a morning meeting on a snowy Wednesday morning prior to the Patriots' Week 14 matchup against the [[Carolina Panthers]].<ref name="ESPN" /> The next day, Thomas told the press that he called the team saying that he was stuck in traffic but was still sent home upon arriving. He also continued to question the perceived motivational aspect of the decision, saying "Motivation is for kindergartners. I'm not a kindergartner."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.espn.com/boston/nfl/news/story?id=4737748|title=Thomas was disciplined earlier in week|work=ESPNBoston.com|first=Mike|last=Reiss|date=2009-12-13|access-date=2009-12-22}}</ref> He was again deactivated for the game against the Panthers, but started the Patriots' Week 15 game against the [[Buffalo Bills]].

Thomas finished the 2009 season with 11 starts in 14 games played, recording 34 tackles and three sacks.

Thomas was released by the Patriots on April 26, 2010, one day after the [[2010 NFL draft]].<ref>{{cite web | title=Patriots release Adalius Thomas | website=New England Patriots | date=2010-04-26 | url=https://www.patriots.com/news/patriots-release-adalius-thomas-114151 | access-date=2025-10-20}}</ref>

'''Abdul Hodge''' (born September 9, 1982) is an [[American football]] coach and former player. He is currently the [[tight end]]s coach at [[Iowa Hawkeyes football|Iowa]], where he played as a 3-time all Big-Ten [[linebacker]]. He was drafted by the [[Green Bay Packers]] in the third round of the [[2006 NFL draft]].

==Early life==
Hodge grew up in [[Fort Lauderdale, Florida]] and attended [[Boyd Anderson High School]] (the same school as college teammate offensive lineman David Walker) where he won 
four [[Varsity letters|letters]] in football, two in [[Track and field|track]], and one in [[basketball]]. In football, he was a three-year starter, and three-time team captain.

Hodge played linebacker for a 9–3 team that reached the state semi-finals. he was selected as an All-American by ''SuperPrep,'' First-team All-State and All-Conference. He was also named [[Broward County]] MVP on defense.

In his high school career, Hodge recorded a total of 308 career tackles, 22 sacks and six interceptions. He also had eight fumble recoveries and fumbles turned for touchdowns. He had over 100 tackles in each of his final three prep seasons. Hodge's best time of 4.5 seconds in the [[40-yard dash]].

==College career==
After being recruited by Iowa linebackers coach [[Bret Bielema]], Hodge attended the University of Iowa, where he majored in [[communication studies]] and was a member of the [[National Honor Society]]. He was also one of five seniors selected to the 2005 Leadership Council and served as a captain that season. At Iowa, Hodge played under head coach [[Kirk Ferentz]] and defensive coordinator [[Norm Parker]].

After redshirting in 2001, Hodge played in all 13 games of the Iowa's conference championship [[2002 Iowa Hawkeyes football team|2002 season]], coming mostly on special teams and as a backup linebacker. In his first game as a Hawkeye, he recorded three solo tackles and three assists in the week one over [[Akron Zips football|Akron]]. He had six solo tackles and two assists in win over [[Purdue Boilermakers football|Purdue]], and later had five solo tackles in win over [[Northwestern Wildcats football|Northwestern]], including a quarterback sack and a quarterback pressure. Hodge recorded four solo tackles and two assists against [[2002 USC Trojans football team|USC]] in the [[2003 Orange Bowl|Orange Bowl]].

In [[2003 Iowa Hawkeyes football team|2003]], Hodge started all 13 games of the season at [[middle linebacker]], earning [[2003 All-Big Ten Conference football team|first-team all-Big Ten]] recognition and leading the conference in tackles as a sophomore. He finished the season with 141 tackles, 9 tackles for loss, 2 [[quarterback sack]]s, 2 [[Fumble|forced fumbles]], and 3 pass break-ups. At [[2003 Ohio State Buckeyes football team|Ohio State]], he recorded eight solo tackles and eight assists for career high 16 tackles. Hodge recorded five solo tackles in win over Penn State, and added a 47-yard fumble return and had one pass break-up. He recorded four solo tackles and four assists in [[2004 Outback Bowl|Outback Bowl]] win over [[Florida Gators football|Florida]].

In [[2004 Iowa Hawkeyes football team|2004]], Hodge started all 12 games at linebacker, again earning [[2004 All-Big Ten Conference football team|first-team all-Big Ten]] honors with fellow Iowa linebacker [[Chad Greenway]] as the Hawkeyes were co-champions of the [[2004 Big Ten Conference football season|Big Ten]]. His season totals included a team-best 116 tackles, including 79 solo  and 37 assists; Hodge also had 4.5 tackles for loss and three QB sacks, four pass break-ups, two fumble recoveries and one forced fumble. In the win over Wisconsin to clinch a share of the Big Ten title, Hodge led the team with 11 tackles, including seven solo. Hodge set a [[Capital One Bowl]] record in [[Capital One Bowl#2005|2005]] with 16 tackles against [[2004 LSU Tigers football team|LSU]].

In [[2005 Iowa Hawkeyes football team|2005]], Hodge was named to several pre-season awards watchlists, including: the [[Bronko Nagurski Trophy]] watch list, the [[Lott Trophy]] watch list, the [[Dick Butkus Award]] watch list, and the [[Chuck Bednarik Award|Bednarik Award]] watch list. After the season, he earned [[2005 All-Big Ten Conference football team|all-Big Ten]] honors for the third time. He was named first-team defensive All-America by [[Phil Steele's]] ''College Football Preview'', second-team All-America by ''Athlon Sports,'' second-team All-America by [[Rivals.com]], third-team All-America by Nationalchamps.net, No. 4 inside linebacker by ''[[The Sporting News]]'', and third-team All-America by collegesportsreport.com. In the win over Illinois he recorded a career-best 18 tackles, including 11 solo, to earn Big Ten Defensive Player of the week honors. Against Florida in the [[2006 Outback Bowl]], Hodge set an Iowa bowl record and [[Outback Bowl]] record with 19 tackles, including 14 solo, he also had one tackle for loss.

Hodge's 158 total tackles in 2005 ranked best for the team during the season, best in the Big Ten, second best all-time at Iowa for a single season, and third in the country.

While at Iowa, he led the Big Ten and ranked third in the nation in tackles per game, ranked third in the nation in solo tackles per game, tied for fifth in the Big Ten in forced [[fumble]]s, and tied for ninth in recovered fumbles. Hodge ranks [[Iowa Hawkeyes football statistical leaders#Tackles|third in career tackles with 453]].

'''Abdul Salaam''' (born '''Larry James Faulk'''; August 12, 1953 – October 8, 2024) was an American professional [[American football|football]] player who played [[defensive tackle]] for the [[New York Jets]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL).<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/S/SalaAb20.htm|title=Abdul Salaam|publisher=Football-Reference.com}}</ref> He was a member of a [[defensive line]] known as the "[[New York Sack Exchange]]".

==Background==
Salaam was born Larry James Faulk in [[New Brockton, Alabama]], in 1953. He grew up in [[Cincinnati, Ohio]], where he played [[baseball]] and [[basketball]] as well as football at [[Woodward High School (Cincinnati, Ohio)|Woodward High School]].<ref name = Sandomir>{{cite news|url = https://www.nytimes.com/2024/10/13/sports/football/abdul-salaam-dead.html|title = Abdul Salaam, Quiet Member of the Jets' 'Sack Exchange,' Dies at 71|last = Sandomir|first = Richard|date = October 13, 2024|accessdate = October 13, 2024|newspaper = [[The New York Times]]|url-access = limited}}</ref> In 1970 his first child, LaTonia allen was born to Karen Allen In 1972, he married Debbie Rawls, whom he had known since childhood; they had two sons.<ref name = Sandomir/>

==College career==
Salaam majored in business at [[Kent State University]], while also playing both [[nose guard]] and [[Linebacker]] with [[Kent State Golden Flashes football|Kent State's]] "Carat Gold" defense. He earned first-team All-[[Mid-American Conference]] three straight seasons.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://einside.kent.edu/?type=art&id=92181|title=Glory Days: Celebrating 90 Years of Kent State Football|publisher=eInside|date=September 7, 2009}}</ref>

==Professional career==
Still known as Larry Faulk when drafted by the New York Jets in the seventh round (188th overall) of the [[1976 NFL draft]], he had converted to Islam and later changed his name to Abdul Salaam, which means "soldier of peace," in 1977, because he wanted serenity in his life.<ref name = Sandomir/><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.barrypopik.com/index.php/new_york_city/entry/new_york_sack_exchange/|title=New York Sack Exchange|author=Jerry Eskenazi|date=October 22, 2002}}</ref>

The Jets went just 3-11 each of Salaam's first two seasons in the [[National Football League]], however, he was soon joined by [[Joe Klecko]], [[Mark Gastineau]], and [[Marty Lyons]] on the Jets' defensive line to form one of the top defensive lines in the NFL, known as the "New York Sack Exchange." The four combined for 66 [[Quarterback sack|sacks]] in [[1981–82 NFL playoffs|1981]] to lead the Jets to their first playoff game since [[AFL playoffs, 1969|1969]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www2.newyorkjets.com/team/all_time/player/679-abdul-salaam |title=Abdul Salaam |publisher=New York Jets Yearbook |year=1983 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20090220165037/http://www.newyorkjets.com/team/all_time/player/679-abdul-salaam |archivedate=2009-02-20 }}</ref>

In November 1981, Salaam, Gastineau, Klecko, and Lyons were invited to ring the ceremonial opening bell at the [[New York Stock Exchange]] that served as the inspiration for their nickname.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.nydailynews.com/sports/football/jets/2008/09/06/2008-09-06_jets_defense_looking_to_regain_glory_day.html |title=Jets defense looking to regain glory days of Sack Exchange |publisher=Nydailynews.com |date=2008-09-06 |accessdate=2010-08-13 | location=New York | first=Rich | last=Cimini}}</ref>

The Jets made the playoffs again in [[1982–83 NFL playoffs|1982]], losing the [[American Football Conference|AFC]] Championship game to the [[Miami Dolphins]]. The only game Salaam appeared in for the Jets in 1983 was the final game of the season, a 34–14 loss to the Dolphins in Miami that brought the Jets' record to 7–9. Following the season, he was traded with [[Kenny Neil]] to the [[San Diego Chargers]] for a [[1984 NFL draft]] second-round pick,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/article/magazine/MAG1121803/2/index.htm|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110603235339/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/article/magazine/MAG1121803/2/index.htm|url-status=dead|archive-date=June 3, 2011|title=A Roundup Of The Week|author=Ivan Maisel|date=February 27, 1984|publisher=[[Sports Illustrated]]}}</ref> but neither player ever made an appearance with his new team. After his NFL career ended, he was a high school football coach.<ref name = Sandomir/>

==Death==
Salaam died at a Cincinnati hospital on October 8, 2024 at the age of 71.<ref name = Sandomir/> He had been dealing with multiple health issues, including [[diabetes]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Cimini |first1=Rich |title=Abdul Salaam, member of Jets' Sack Exchange, dies at 71 |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/41700163/abdul-salaam-member-jets-sack-exchange-dies-71 |access-date=9 October 2024 |publisher=ESPN |date=9 October 2024}}</ref>

'''Adam David Goldberg''' (born August 12, 1980) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was an [[offensive tackle]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Wyoming Cowboys football|Wyoming Cowboys]]. Goldberg was signed by the NFL's [[Minnesota Vikings]] in 2003, played for the Vikings from 2003 to 2005, and played for the [[St. Louis Rams]] from 2006 to 2011.

==Early life==
Goldberg was born in [[Edina, Minnesota]]. His father is [[Jewish]], and he considers himself Jewish, despite having been raised as Catholic (his mother's Christian faith).<ref>[https://www.jta.org/2012/09/05/arts-entertainment/six-degrees-no-bacon/the-non-goy-gridiron-gang-9-jewish-nfl-players-2012-2013-edition The Non-Goy Gridiron Gang: 9 Jewish NFL Players (2012-2013 edition) | Jewish Telegraphic Agency<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref><ref>{{cite news |url=http://njjewishnews.com/kaplanskorner/2008/11/26/nfl-update/ |author=Ron Kaplan |title=NFL Update » Kaplan's Korner on Jews and Sports |publisher=[[New Jersey Jewish News]] |date=November 26, 2008 |accessdate=March 13, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130629120214/http://njjewishnews.com/kaplanskorner/2008/11/26/nfl-update/ |archive-date=June 29, 2013 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>[https://www.clevelandjewishnews.com/news/local/jews-in-football/article_f95120b0-dcba-11e1-b1b5-001a4bcf887a.html Jews in football | News | clevelandjewishnews.com<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=May 31, 2011 |title=On To The Next One: Adam Goldberg |url=https://www.businessinsider.com/on-to-the-next-one-adam-goldberg-2011-6 |access-date=2023-03-28 |website=Business Insider |language=en-US}}</ref>

At [[Edina High School]], Goldberg, referred to as "Barch" and "El Barcho Solamente," was a Second-team All-State and All-Metro selection his senior season. He played both offensive and [[defensive line]]. His senior season, he recorded 95 tackles (19 solo) and 76 assists.

==College career==
Goldberg is a [[University of Wyoming]] graduate. He became only the third junior in University of Wyoming football history to be elected a team captain when he was voted a captain by his teammates in the spring of 2001. He was Honorable Mention [[All-America]] and two-time First-team All-[[Mountain West Conference]]. He started 44 of 45 career games. He graduated with a finance degree.

==Professional career==

===Minnesota Vikings===
Goldberg spent 2003 season on Minnesota Vikings. practice squad. In 2004, he started the last six games of the season and two postseason contests. In 2005, he started 12 games at right tackle.

===St. Louis Rams===
On September 2, 2006, the Vikings traded Goldberg to the [[St. Louis Rams]] for the seventh-round selection (209th overall) in the [[2008 NFL draft]].<ref>{{cite web | last = Pasquarelli | first = Len | title = Rams hope Goldberg can fill Pace's shoes at left tackle | publisher = ESPN | date = November 17, 2006 | url = https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=2666030 | access-date = April 23, 2008 }}</ref> In 2006, he played in final 15 games of the season with two starts for the Rams.

The following season, 2007, he played in four games with two starts before being placed on reserve/injured list with a left knee injury suffered in Week 4. An [[unrestricted free agent]] in the 2009 offseason, Goldberg was re-signed by the Rams on March 20, 2009, to a two-year, $1.8 million contract.<ref>Caplan, Adam. (March 22, 2009). [http://profootball.scout.com/a.z?s=127&p=9&c=2&cid=849555&nid=4245471  OL Re-Signs With STL] Scout.com. Retrieved May 3, 2009.</ref>

'''Aaron Scott Walker''' (born March 14, 1980) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[tight end]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL).  Walker played [[college football]] for the [[Florida Gators football|Florida Gators]], and thereafter he played in the NFL for the [[San Francisco 49ers]] and [[St. Louis Rams]].

== Early life ==

Walker was born in [[Titusville, Florida]], in 1980.<ref name="pfrprofile">{{Cite web |title=Aaron Walker Stats, Height, Weight, Position, Draft, College |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/W/WalkAa00.htm |access-date=2025-10-05 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref>  He attended [[Astronaut High School]] in Titusville,<ref name="dbfprofile">databaseFootball.com, Players, {{usurped|1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20110610114609/http://www.databasefootball.com/players/playerpage.htm?ilkid=WALKEAAR01  Aaron Walker]}}.  Retrieved September 23, 2010.</ref> and played high school football for the Astronaut War Eagles.<ref name="ufprofile">GatorZone.com, Football History, 2002 Roster, [http://web.gatorzone.com/football/bios.php?year=2002&bio=walker_a.html  Aaron Walker] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120402034512/http://web.gatorzone.com/football/bios.php?year=2002&bio=walker_a.html |date=April 2, 2012 }}.  Retrieved April 7, 2011.</ref>  As a senior tight end in 1997, Walker caught thirty-six for 497 yards, while also recording eighty-two tackles and fourteen [[quarterback sack]]s as a [[defensive end]].<ref name=ufprofile/>  He received Florida Class 4A all-state honors and was recognized as a high school [[All-American]] by PrepStar and Super Prep.<ref name=ufprofile/>  Walker was also a letterman in [[basketball]] and [[baseball]].<ref name=ufprofile/>

== College career ==

Walker accepted an athletic scholarship to attend the [[University of Florida]] in Gainesville, Florida,<ref name=ufprofile/> where he played for coach [[Steve Spurrier]] and coach [[Ron Zook]]'s [[Florida Gators football|Gators]] teams from [[1999 Florida Gators football team|1999]] to [[2002 Florida Gators football team|2002]].<ref name="ufmediaguide">''[http://web.gatorzone.com/football/media/2011/media_guide.pdf  2011 Florida Gators Football Media Guide] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120402035222/http://web.gatorzone.com/football/media/2011/media_guide.pdf |date=April 2, 2012 }}'', University Athletic Association, Gainesville, Florida, pp. 85, 97, 99, 186 (2011).  Retrieved August 31, 2011.</ref>  Walker was a second-team [[List of All-SEC football teams|All-Southeastern Conference]] (SEC) selection after his senior season in 2002.<ref name=ufmediaguide/>  In his four-year college career, he played in forty-seven games, started twenty-nine of them, and caught fifty-six passes for 716 yards and nine touchdowns.<ref name=ufprofile/>

He played [[college football]] for the [[Notre Dame Fighting Irish football|Notre Dame Fighting Irish]] and [[Kent State Golden Flashes football|Kent State Golden Flashes]]. ==Early life== Elam opted to attend [[Cardinal Newman High School (West Palm Beach, Florida)|Cardinal Newman High School]], instead of enrolling at [[Suncoast Community High School]].{{citation|url=https://www.clevescene.com/64-and-counting/archives/2009/08/20/abram-elam-from-scenes-archives|title=Abram Elam: From Scene's Archives|publisher=Scene|date=August 20, 2009|accessdate=February 19, 2020|archive-date=July 11, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200711125628/https://www.clevescene.com/64-and-counting/archives/2009/08/20/abram-elam-from-scenes-archives|url-status=dead}} He was a two-way player at [[quarterback]] and [[defensive back]]. As a senior, he registered 1,087 passing yards, 12 passing [[touchdown]]s, 542 rushing yards and 11 rushing [[touchdown]]s. He received All-state, Palm Beach County Player of the Year and Ft. Lauderdale [[Sun-Sentinel]] Offensive Player of the Year honors. In [[basketball]], he helped his team win two state Class AAA titles and was named to the All-conference team. He was the first four-year [[Letterman (sports)|letterman]] in two sports in school history. ==College career== Elam accepted a football scholarship from the [[University of Notre Dame]].
